newsitem.title: FRANCE: Slow French growth shows task for finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Slow French growth shows task for finance minister.

text.p: France's new Socialist finance minister took office on Thursday with the unenviable task of getting public finances into shape for European monetary union after promising to spare voters further economic austerity.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn took over a newly merged finance and industry portfolio the same day as the INSEE statistics office released data showing economic growth made a relatively lacklustre start in the first quarter of 1997.

The 48-year-old appointed by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Wednesday and seen by some in the financial markets as a fairly pragmatic and pro-European left-winger, inherits an economy in the test year for joining a single euro currency.

In a brief handover ceremony at the ministry, he refrained from specifics on policy, saying his aim was to keep "some of the policies which were pursued by our predecessors, which in part seem to us to be going in the right direction". But he added, "obviously some policy shifts will emerge".

Some economists say data showing a 0.2 percent rise in gross domestic product for the first three months of 1997 augurs badly for the full year, although financial market analysts have long been saying a pick-up was likely in the latter half of the year.
Strauss-Kahn, principal author of Socialist economic policy, will clearly have his hands full.
There was already considerable speculation about the ability of the previous centre-right government to meet its objectives on public deficit control.

Strauss-Kahn has the additional task of reconciling deficit control requirements which go hand-in-hand with a commitment to join monetary union in 1999 with an election pledge to promote growth and jobs and avoid further public spending cutbacks.

The centre-right government ousted in Sunday's parliamentary election had forecast economic growth of at least 2.3 percent in 1997 and said it would limit the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to qualify for monetary union.

The Socialists, who dominate the new coalition with Greens and Communists, have accused their predecessors of choking consumer spending, and growth as a result, by hiking value-added tax and slamming the brakes too hard on public spending.
What could prove crucial for Strauss-Kahn is an audit of state finances planned by Jospin. The date has yet to be set.
He and Jospin have to judge whether the public deficit can be limited this year to three percent of GDP and, if not, what overshoot they can live with and defend with European partners.

That balancing act will be closely watched by Germany, seen as the shrine of fiscal rectitude on the road to the euro, but Strauss-Kahn's message was: "There is no reason for Germany to be worried, so there is no reason for me to reassure them".

During the election campaign, the Socialists made it clear they backed launching the euro on time in 1999 but said people should not suffer more austerity based on a rigid, arithmetical view that the deficit had to hit precisely 3.0 percent.
Pressure on finances could mount significantly if the new coalition gets demands for a big rise in pay for several million civil servants and a big hike in the national minimum wage.

Trade unions universally opposed the previous government's decision to impose a 2.8 percent pay increase spread over this year and next and are expected to renew their demands for at least a "catch-up payment" after a pay freeze in 1996.

In the background to all of this, prospects for increased economic growth remain cloudy. The data on Thursday showed that business investment fell 1.3 percent in the first quarter of the year, while household spending rose 0.4 percent.
Some analysts felt the first quarter could be the last of several weak ones but scepticism about the outlook prevails.

"I honestly don't see anything in the figures to think growth will exceed two percent this year," said Joanne Perez, a strategist at Merrill Lynch. "The window of opportunity (for the Socialists) is quite short."
